extracted.intended_audience: aspiring stand-up comedians, comedy writers, and performers learning joke structure and stagecraft
extracted.subtask_description: A glossary-style how-to reference of terms, concepts, and informal standards for writing and performing stand-up comedy, covering joke structure, stagecraft, material grading, club logistics, and common anti-patterns.

rubrics_metrics.name: TCR
rubrics_metrics.description: Abbreviation for Target Assumption, Connector, and Reinterpretation, hence TCR, as defined in Greg Dean's Joke Structure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use TCR when analyzing or building jokes with Dean's model. See jokes, joke diagram, and Joke Prospector Writing System.

rubrics_metrics.name: telegraphing
rubrics_metrics.description: Causing the audience to guess the Punchline before it's delivered, which usually means the Setup has too much information or an acting choice that leads the audience prematurely to the idea of the punchline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Telegraphing is an anti-pattern to avoid; aim for misdirection instead. See joke structure and misdirection. (Submitted by Scotty Meltzer.)

rubrics_metrics.name: throw away
rubrics_metrics.description: To place little performing emphasis on jokes which are usually considered important.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use when intentionally downplaying a line to affect audience reaction or pacing.

rubrics_metrics.name: time slot
rubrics_metrics.description: Spot on comedy room or club lineups which designates the time and length of time comedians get to perform.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Know your time slot (see lineup, open mics, and regulars) and prepare material lengths accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: timing
rubrics_metrics.description: (1) The tempo, rhythm developed between the comedian and the audience while performing stand-up comedy. (2) Figuring out at home the length of time a routine or show will take.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Timing affects laughs and pacing — practice for rhythm, watch feedback loop and comedy timing.

rubrics_metrics.name: topic
rubrics_metrics.description: Large starting single idea about something wrong from which entire routines or shows are written. (Not to be confused with Premise which is a narrower idea stated as a negative opinion about a subject.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use topic to build a set; see routines, comedy voice, and joke writing.

rubrics_metrics.name: topical jokes
rubrics_metrics.description: Comedy material based on current events, cultural trends, fades, and politics usually done on late night talk shows and sketch shows.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Common on one-liners, political humor, and roasts; be mindful of shelf-life.

rubrics_metrics.name: topper
rubrics_metrics.description: Antiquated term referring to a joke building off a previous joke.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See tag, joke, and capper; modern term often 'tag'.

rubrics_metrics.name: traditional clubs
rubrics_metrics.description: Professional stand-up comedy clubs and venues that use an MC and/or opener, feature or middle, and headliner comedians as the format for their shows.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See showcase clubs for formats and expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: triple up
rubrics_metrics.description: To perform in three comedy clubs, rooms or open mics in one night.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A strategy for increasing stage time; see double up, open mics, and stage time.

rubrics_metrics.name: unexpected interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: In Greg Dean's joke structure, the unexpected interpretation of the Connector becomes the mechanism the Reinterpretation, expressed in the Punchline to create surprise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Central to creating surprise; see expected interpretation, Reinterpretation, Connector, and Target Assumption.

rubrics_metrics.name: unpaid regular
rubrics_metrics.description: Comedians who frequently perform at a particular showcase comedy club, but does not get paid because they are getting stage time and experience in front of live audiences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stage-time-focused role; see regular, paid regular, and stage time. Example: After months of open mics, someone may become an unpaid regular.

rubrics_metrics.name: variety performer
rubrics_metrics.description: Comedians who do comedy along with other performing skills, such as juggling, guitar, magic, ventriloquism, props, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Useful for different types of gigs and venues.

rubrics_metrics.name: venue
rubrics_metrics.description: Any space, room, stage, or club used for presenting stand-up comedy shows.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand venue size and audience when planning material and delivery.

rubrics_metrics.name: walking ovation
rubrics_metrics.description: Applause while the audience leaving the room or club.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See applause break and standing ovation; indicates strong sustained approval.

rubrics_metrics.name: warm up
rubrics_metrics.description: (1) Before a show when comedians prepare themselves to go on stage by doing light physical exercise, rituals, going through the set order, making up jokes for entrance, etc. (2) At the beginning of shows, when comedians work the crowd with material, requests for applause, crowd work, etc. to unify the audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Warm-ups help create a unified laughing audience and prepare performer energy.

rubrics_metrics.name: week gigs
rubrics_metrics.description: Comedy jobs with performances on Thursday through Sunday nights.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See traditional clubs and weekend gigs; scheduling consideration for touring comedians.

rubrics_metrics.name: weekend gigs
rubrics_metrics.description: Comedy club jobs performed on Friday, Saturday, and sometimes Sunday nights.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: High-demand slots; see traditional clubs and week gigs.

rubrics_metrics.name: wind down
rubrics_metrics.description: After shows when comedians come down from the excitement and stress of performing by getting something to eat, drinking or using drugs, or socializing until they are calm or numb enough to be able to sleep.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Self-care practice post-performance.

rubrics_metrics.name: wordplay
rubrics_metrics.description: Verbal wit based on the meanings and ambiguities of words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes puns, double entendres, connectors; example: routines filled with clever wordplay get laughs. See ambiguity, joke, pun, double entendre, and connector.

rubrics_metrics.name: X rated material
rubrics_metrics.description: Jokes or routines with foul language, graphic sex, toilet, and mucus references which can be very offensive to average sensibilities and cannot be done on network TV.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Also called blue material or toilet material; choose based on audience and venue.

rubrics_metrics.name: 1st Story
rubrics_metrics.description: The scene imagined in audience's minds based upon receiving a joke's Setup; one of the five joke structure mechanisms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used in Greg Dean's method; sets the Target Assumption. See Joke Prospector Writing System.

rubrics_metrics.name: 2nd Story
rubrics_metrics.description: The scene imagined in audience's minds based upon receiving a joke's Punchline; one of the five joke structure mechanisms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reframes the setup into a new scene — essential for punchline impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: 3 POVs
rubrics_metrics.description: POVs (Points of View): Narrator POV, Self POV, and Character POV — performance roles in stand-up storytelling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comedians shift between these to construct scenes; see Anatomy of Funny Storytelling.

rubrics_metrics.name: 3-5 and 10
rubrics_metrics.description: Three most common lengths of routines or shows, in minutes, which comedians need to have prepared and ready to perform upon request.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Have material prepared for 3-5 minute and 10-minute spots for open mics and showcases.

rubrics_metrics.name: 4 Cs
rubrics_metrics.description: Abbreviation for Clubs, Colleges, Cruise ships, and Corporations — four venues where stand-up comedians can get work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this to plan markets for booking gigs.

rubrics_metrics.name: 4th wall
rubrics_metrics.description: Convention that imagines a wall existing between performers and their audience; in stand-up, scenes where POVs live in that environment unaware there's an audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Useful concept for scene work and act-outs. See Anatomy of Funny Storytelling.

rubrics_metrics.name: 5 joke mechanisms
rubrics_metrics.description: In the Greg Dean model, mechanisms connecting Setup and Punchline: 1st Story, Target Assumption, Connector, Reinterpretation, and 2nd Story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Framework for analyzing and constructing jokes; see Greg Dean's Joke Structure and Joke Prospector.

rubrics_metrics.name: 5 LPMs
rubrics_metrics.description: Abbreviation for Laughs Per Minute. 5 or more laughs per minute is the professional standard for stand-up comedy shows.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use LPM as a rough performance metric when assessing or pacing a set; see routines and laughs per minute.

rubrics_metrics.name: A material
rubrics_metrics.description: In the ABCs of comedy material rating system, A is the funniest jokes in routines or funniest routines in shows.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use A material for closers or strongest spots; example sequencing: start with B, do crowd work, end with A.

rubrics_metrics.name: ABCs
rubrics_metrics.description: Rating system that gives values to jokes within routines, or routines within shows with A being the best.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use ABCs to grade material effectiveness; helps plan set order and edits.

rubrics_metrics.name: act out
rubrics_metrics.description: (1) Scene work in a stand-up comedy routine. (2) A scene where the comedian portrays Narrator POV, Self POV, and Character POV.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Technique to bring scenes to life; coined by Judy Carter. See scene work and Anatomy of Funny Storytelling.

rubrics_metrics.name: ad-lib
rubrics_metrics.description: Spontaneously stating jokes within a scripted routine or show.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Often used in response to crowd or for improvisational bits; relates to improv.

rubrics_metrics.name: age out
rubrics_metrics.description: Point at which older comedians cannot get work because the younger generation of audiences don’t attend their shows.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Career risk to monitor; tied to trends and audience demographics.

rubrics_metrics.name: alternative interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: An unexpected, yet compatible meaning of a Connector other than the Target Assumption; creates surprise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key to Reinterpretation in Greg Dean's system — 'what creates surprise is an unexpected alternative interpretation.'

rubrics_metrics.name: ambiguity
rubrics_metrics.description: (1) Anything open to more than one interpretation. (2) In joke structure, an ambiguity, usually in setups, is anything that can have more than one meaning and becomes the Connector.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use ambiguity deliberately as the Connector to enable misdirection and punchlines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anatomy of Funny Storytelling
rubrics_metrics.description: Greg Dean’s model of the three performance roles/POVs used in stand-up comedy storytelling: Narrator POV, Self POV, and Character POV.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Study to understand how POV shifts support jokes and scenes; see story structure and act out.

rubrics_metrics.name: applau / applause break
rubrics_metrics.description: Applau: a single clap in a crowded venue. Applause break: when an audience spontaneously claps in approval for a joke or routine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applause break indicates strong positive reaction; applau is described humorously. See applause and applause break.

rubrics_metrics.name: assumption / assumptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Beliefs people form without proof used to fill in ambiguous or incomplete information from setups or punchlines; in jokes, assumptions produce mental scenarios (1st/2nd Story).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Target Assumption is a key element in joke misdirection; managing audience assumptions is essential to craft surprise.

rubrics_metrics.name: attitude
rubrics_metrics.description: (1) A fixed way of thinking or feeling about someone or something. (2) In stand-up, the expression of one negative emotion or judgment repeatedly used toward every subject in jokes and routines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Developing a consistent comedic attitude can define comic voice.

rubrics_metrics.name: availability dates / avails
rubrics_metrics.description: Calendar sent to bookers to indicate when the comedian can accept comedy gigs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Send clear avails to bookers to facilitate booking; administrative best practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: B material
rubrics_metrics.description: In the ABCs, B is the second-best jokes in a routine, or second-best routines within a show.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: B material can be used to open and to test tags; sequence with BCAs ordering.

rubrics_metrics.name: BCAs
rubrics_metrics.description: The most effective order for placing jokes within routines or routines within shows: B first, C in the middle, and A to close.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use BCAs to maintain momentum, introduce new material (C) in the middle, then close strong with A.

rubrics_metrics.name: bit
rubrics_metrics.description: A section of stand-up comedy routines or shows or a short routine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bits are building blocks of sets; trim or remove bits that slow the show.

rubrics_metrics.name: bitters
rubrics_metrics.description: Angry resentful state of mind some comedians get when they've had a long career but never made it big; feel overlooked.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Awareness of emotional pitfalls for career longevity.

rubrics_metrics.name: blank, going
rubrics_metrics.description: While performing when comedians forget their jokes and feel as if they have forgotten everything they've even known.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Related to flop sweat and rehearsal process; prepare recovery lines and practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: blue material
rubrics_metrics.description: Jokes, routines, or shows using graphic sexual, scatological, and swear words; not appropriate for network television.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish from clean material; know venue expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: bomb / die / dog it / flop / flop sweat / crickets / eat it / suck / tank
rubrics_metrics.description: Terms describing performing shows or jokes that get few or no laughs and the resulting performer reactions (e.g., flop sweat).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize bombing as part of process; analyze why (material, timing, venue) and adjust. See synonyms and coping strategies.

rubrics_metrics.name: booked / booking / booker
rubrics_metrics.description: Booked: hired for a comedy gig. Booking: the act of hiring comedians for shows. Booker: person who hires and pays comedians to work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand booking processes and relationships with bookers/PA representation.

rubrics_metrics.name: bringer / bringer room / bringer show
rubrics_metrics.description: Rooms or shows that require comedians to bring paying audience members in order to get stage time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Often early-late and lower-quality shows; plan carefully and warn friends about late slots.

rubrics_metrics.name: bumped / drop in
rubrics_metrics.description: Bumped: being pushed to a later time slot. Drop in: when a famous comedian unexpectedly enters and is put on stage, causing others to be bumped.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be flexible; know your status (paid regulars vs unpaid) to anticipate being bumped.

rubrics_metrics.name: C material
rubrics_metrics.description: In the ABCs, C is the weakest jokes in routines or weakest routines within a show.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Place C material between stronger bits or use as experimental content; see BCAs and hammock/sandwich strategies.

rubrics_metrics.name: call-in a show / phone in
rubrics_metrics.description: When a comedian gives the minimum effort to a performance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid — audiences notice low effort; aim for engaged performing.

rubrics_metrics.name: callback
rubrics_metrics.description: Repeating the punchline from a previously performed joke earlier in the routine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effective device to build momentum and payoff later in the set; practice placement.

rubrics_metrics.name: capper / closing line / closer
rubrics_metrics.description: Capper: antiquated term for final joke. Closer/closing line: comedian’s final joke or routine intended to end with the biggest laugh.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: End with your strongest material; consider audience exit effects (walking ovation).

rubrics_metrics.name: catchphrase
rubrics_metrics.description: Common phrase repeatedly delivered with unusual emphasis that becomes a comedian's verbal trademark.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Can build recognizability but risks hackiness if overused.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character POV
rubrics_metrics.description: One of three perceptual positions when comedians act out scenes and portray someone else.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Character POV for act-outs and scene specificity; see Narrator POV and Self POV.

rubrics_metrics.name: chops
rubrics_metrics.description: Description of comedians with a great deal of experience who handle difficult audience situations with ease.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chops are developed through stage time and varied experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: clapter
rubrics_metrics.description: Joke designed to get an audience to applaud and agree, rather than laugh; term usually used negatively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid relying on clapter if you want real laughter; be wary of applause-for-agreement lines.

rubrics_metrics.name: clean material
rubrics_metrics.description: Jokes with no curse words or inappropriate subjects suitable for network television.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Useful for certain gigs and television; maintain versions for different audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: comeback / heckler line
rubrics_metrics.description: Prepared insult jokes and quick replies to handle hecklers and interruptions to shut them down or turn them into laughs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Memorize versatile heckler lines and comebacks; practice delivery to defuse or own the moment.

rubrics_metrics.name: comedian / comic / comedienne
rubrics_metrics.description: Someone who seeks to entertain people by making them laugh; terms vary by gender and nuance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinctions: a 'comic' uses jokes; a 'comedian' says things funny; cultivate your persona and voice.

rubrics_metrics.name: comedian’s comedian / comic’s comic
rubrics_metrics.description: Comedians other comedians most admire or emulate; performers highly respected by peers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Often stylistically ambitious or influential even if not mainstream famous.

rubrics_metrics.name: comedy timing / comic timing
rubrics_metrics.description: Tempo, rhythm, and emphasis of material and response in a feedback loop between comedians and their audiences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Essential performance skill; study exemplars and practice timing with audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: comic’s clichés / hack / hacky
rubrics_metrics.description: Overused topics, premises, and jokes or performers relying on clichés and stale routines; 'hack' is derogatory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid hacky material; prioritize originality and audience connection.

rubrics_metrics.name: common knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: (1) Information generally shared by most people. (2) In stand-up, information within jokes the audience must be familiar with to get the joke.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure setups rely on common knowledge or explain succinctly to avoid confusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: compere / emcee / MC / host
rubrics_metrics.description: Person who runs shows, introduces performers, does housekeeping, and warms up the crowd.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good hosts manage transitions, announcements, and energy; being a host is a way to get stage time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Connector
rubrics_metrics.description: Joke structure mechanism at the center of comedy: 1 thing with at least 2 interpretations; the ambiguity that links Setup and Punchline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Connector as the pivot for misdirection; fully explained in Greg Dean's books. See ambiguity and Target Assumption.

rubrics_metrics.name: cord / microphone / mic cord
rubrics_metrics.description: The electrical cable attached to the microphone that plugs into venue sound equipment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Technical stage consideration; know setup and safety.

rubrics_metrics.name: cotton mouth / dry mouth
rubrics_metrics.description: Condition of low saliva due to performing anxiety or substance use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bring water on stage; manage anxiety and substances to reduce effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: crowd work
rubrics_metrics.description: When comedians ask questions of the audience then banter with the intent to find laughs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop interpersonal skills and quick thinking; crowd work can create unique set moments and gauge audience mood.

rubrics_metrics.name: delivery
rubrics_metrics.description: Style of intonation, inflection, pace, timing, and character idiosyncrasies when presenting material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Delivery can make or break written jokes; align cadence and emphasis with punchlines.

rubrics_metrics.name: double entendre / pun / groaner
rubrics_metrics.description: Word or phrase open to two interpretations, often risqué; groaner often refers to a pun that elicits groans.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use sparingly; puns can be effective but risk groans if overused.

rubrics_metrics.name: double take
rubrics_metrics.description: Physical reaction where a comedian looks back quickly to show shock or disbelief, used for comedic effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classic physical comedy technique; timing is critical.

rubrics_metrics.name: double up
rubrics_metrics.description: Performing in two comedy rooms or clubs in a single night.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maximizes stage time; manage logistics and energy.

rubrics_metrics.name: downstage center / DSC
rubrics_metrics.description: Stage location closest to the audience at the center; DSC abbreviation used in stage directions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be mindful of mic placement and exits; 'leave the mic' properly.

rubrics_metrics.name: dramedy
rubrics_metrics.description: Entertainment balancing elements of drama and comedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Useful hybrid format for certain gigs and writing projects.

rubrics_metrics.name: drop out / fill in
rubrics_metrics.description: Drop out: comedians cancel or fail to show. Fill in: replacing someone with little notice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain availability and be prepared to fill in; communicate with bookers.

rubrics_metrics.name: DSC
rubrics_metrics.description: Abbreviation for downstage center.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stage direction shorthand; ensure you know stage blocking.

rubrics_metrics.name: dying
rubrics_metrics.description: How comedians feel when doing a show that gets no or few laughs; 'I'm dying up here.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize performance slumps and analyze causes (material, timing, audience).

rubrics_metrics.name: eccentric
rubrics_metrics.description: Funny people with unique character or style that move outside of norms even for comedians.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinctive personas can attract niche audiences; study Andy Kaufman, Jim Carrey as examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: edgy / dark material / hurt line
rubrics_metrics.description: Material dealing with hurtful subjects but maintaining comedic tone without crossing into drama.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Edge requires careful navigation of the 'hurt line' — know your audience and intent.

rubrics_metrics.name: expectation / expected interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: The desired result established by setups: the Target Assumption and expected interpretation of the Connector which creates misdirection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Set expectations clearly then subvert them to produce surprise; see 1st Story, 2nd Story, and surprise.

rubrics_metrics.name: fall flat
rubrics_metrics.description: Jokes, routines, or shows that get less of a response than expected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze and adjust material, delivery or placement when things fall flat.

rubrics_metrics.name: feature
rubrics_metrics.description: The second or middle comedian in the traditional three-comedian lineup.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Feature sets (e.g., 30 minutes) require more developed material than opener slots.

rubrics_metrics.name: gag / gag file
rubrics_metrics.description: Gag: a joke or funny prank. Gag file: organized collection of jokes and routines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain a gag file for material development and edits over time.

rubrics_metrics.name: gelotophobia
rubrics_metrics.description: An extreme or irrational fear of being laughed at.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Related to stage fright and performance anxiety; seek strategies to manage fear.

rubrics_metrics.name: get the light
rubrics_metrics.description: Signal given that only one minute remains or it's time to end the show; 'respect the light.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Always respect show timing and leave the stage when signaled.

rubrics_metrics.name: gig
rubrics_metrics.description: A show business job; first paid gig likely at a comedy room.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Track gigs, avails, and booking contacts; treat each gig professionally.

rubrics_metrics.name: graph
rubrics_metrics.description: Visual device with dots used to evaluate effectiveness of jokes to determine placement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quantitative aid to analyze which jokes get the best reactions; pair with ABCs/BCAs.

rubrics_metrics.name: green room / green room personality
rubrics_metrics.description: Location in venues where comedians gather; green room personality describes off-stage demeanor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be professional offstage; green room behavior affects reputation and bookings.

rubrics_metrics.name: groaner
rubrics_metrics.description: (1) A joke, usually a pun, that causes the audience to groan. (2) Audience members who groan instead of laugh.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Groaners can be contagious; use them sparingly and manage audience tone.

rubrics_metrics.name: guest set or spot
rubrics_metrics.description: Courtesy five-to-ten-minute shows offered by clubs so accomplished comedians can audition live.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use guest sets to showcase material and audition for longer spots.

rubrics_metrics.name: hack
rubrics_metrics.description: Comics who perform overused and cliché topics and jokes with overacted delivery lacking originality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid hack material by developing unique angles, fresh premises, and authentic voice.

rubrics_metrics.name: hammock / sandwich
rubrics_metrics.description: Technique of placing weak or new material between two strong jokes or routines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hammock supports new material and prevents momentum loss; see BCAs.

rubrics_metrics.name: headliner
rubrics_metrics.description: The main act who performs the final and longest set, typically 45–60 minutes and has following to draw audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Headlining requires sustained material, pacing, and audience management.

rubrics_metrics.name: heckler
rubrics_metrics.description: Audience members who talk out loud or make comments and interrupt shows and the comedian's rhythm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Have heckler lines and come-backs ready; train to shut down or incorporate heckles into laughs.

rubrics_metrics.name: housekeeping
rubrics_metrics.description: Duties of the MC to make announcements, promote shows, recognize birthdays, point out exits and restrooms, calm hecklers, sell merchandise, run raffles, give curtain calls, and end shows.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Housekeeping keeps shows running smoothly and sets venue expectations; an essential MC skill.
